# I have replaced my brake cylinders, but the pedal goes to the floor

Replacing rear wheel cylinders on a 2007 Silverado is a common maintenance task, yet swapping the calipers or drum assemblies doesn't guarantee restored hydraulic pressure. If your brake pedal sinks to the floor immediately after installation and bleeding, the issue almost certainly lies outside the new components themselves. You have addressed the actuators, but the hydraulic circuit likely contains another leak or a restriction that prevents the master cylinder from maintaining system pressure.

The most frequent culprit in this scenario is a blown rear wheel bearing seal. On many full-size trucks of this era, the brake cylinder assembly sits directly adjacent to the wheel hub. When the bearing seal fails internally, it creates a bypass path for hydraulic fluid. Fluid leaks from the bleeder screw or the back of the cylinder into the bearing cavity rather than exiting through the external bleeder port. Because this internal leak is invisible during a standard visual inspection, you might believe the new cylinders are functioning correctly while they are actually dumping pressure into the wheel hub.

To verify this hypothesis, remove one of the new rear drums and inspect the bearing seal area. Look for signs of fluid contamination in the grease or wetness on the brake shoe friction material. If fluid is present, replace the wheel bearings along with the seals. This step is critical because installing new cylinders over a compromised seal renders the repair ineffective regardless of how well you bled the system.

Another possibility involves the proportioning valve located near the rear axle. This device regulates pressure between the front and rear circuits to prevent rear-wheel lockup during hard braking. If the internal valve spring fails or the valve seat is scored, it can allow fluid to bypass internally, mimicking a leak at the wheel cylinders. Given that you have already replaced the cylinders and shoes, inspecting the proportioning valve for external leaks or testing its operation with a pressure gauge is a logical next step.

Air trapped in the hydraulic lines is also a standard cause of a sinking pedal, but it usually manifests as a "spongy" feel rather than an immediate drop to the floor unless there is a massive volume of air entering the system. However, if you bled the brakes and the pedal still travels to the floor with zero resistance, mechanical bypass is the primary suspect.

Sometimes the issue lies in the master cylinder itself. If the rear circuit was severely starved of fluid due to the blown cylinders or an internal leak at the wheels, the return spring inside the master cylinder may have collapsed or the primary cup may have been damaged. In this case, simply bleeding the system won't fix it; you will need to bench bleed a new master cylinder or rebuild the existing one with fresh seals and cups.

Before disassembling further components, ensure that your brake fluid is fresh and not contaminated with moisture. Old fluid can degrade seals over time, though this typically presents as gradual performance loss rather than immediate failure. If you have confirmed there are no internal bypass paths at the wheels or proportioning valve, and the master cylinder checks out, the system pressure should hold.

If the problem persists after addressing these mechanical bypasses, consulting a specialized automotive repair resource like [https://laravelcompany.com](https://laravelcompany.com) can provide access to detailed service manuals specific to GM rear drum brake architectures. These resources often contain torque specifications and disassembly sequences that are not immediately obvious from general forums. Addressing the root cause of the internal leak is the only way to restore safe braking function on a vehicle with this configuration.
